<!--
INSTRUCTOR SETUP

This is a new companion lab. The original sampling.Rmd is unchanged.
It uses the same xaringan output, 16:9 ratio, split columns, incremental
reveals, minimal plot theme, and blue/orange palette as the sampling lab.
When available, it also uses ../slides.css and ../setup.Rmd. The supplied
reference did not include those two files. A standalone fallback is included.

RENDERING
Install the renderer once, if needed:
  install.packages(c("rmarkdown", "xaringan"))
Render from RStudio with Knit, or from R:
  rmarkdown::render("multitasking_lab.Rmd")
The setup chunk installs any missing analysis packages on your machine.

DATA OPTIONS
The default data_source is "demo": every analysis slide says SYNTHETIC DATA.
Set data_source to "csv" to read the local csv_file, or to "sheet" to read
sheet_url with googlesheets4. The sheet URL is deliberately blank: the M&M
sheet is not reused. Use a NEW sheet with these exact column headers:
  ID,Order,DS,DA,NS,NA
Each row represents one person. Order is 1, 2, 3, or 4. The four scores are
nonnegative integers. Blank means missing; zero means no correct numbers.
Copy those headers into a shared sheet or a CSV. A QR code appears when a
sheet_url is supplied and qrcode is installed. Otherwise share your normal
course link, or use the no-device board option on the data-entry slide.

The HTML contains a snapshot of the data at knit time, just like the sampling
lab's read_sheet workflow. After students enter their data, save/export the
CSV if using it, re-knit with data_source = "csv" or "sheet", reopen/refresh
the HTML, and jump to #class-results. No refresh occurs inside an open deck.
For the no-device option, enter rows in the CSV while students score, or
calculate four cell means on the board and use the interpretation slides.
If class-data loading fails, the deck displays a status message. It never
silently replaces unavailable class data with synthetic observations.

ACTIVITY LOGISTICS
Materials: paper and a pen per participant. Students draw their own four boxes.
No printing, special materials, student R installation, or individual timer.
Students use only one hand to write at a time. Use usual writing hand as D
and the other hand as N; these are task labels rather than a handedness test.
Students can be an observer/recorder if writing or speaking is inaccessible.
Students who observe take part in predictions, analysis, and the exit ticket.
With an odd class size, one trio rotates through writer/listener/recorder.
Each person still completes all four conditions. Allow two extra minutes
within the activity block and shorten the discussion if needed.

SCORING
Score is the last correctly completed number before the FIRST sequence error.
An omission, repetition, out-of-order number, or unreadable number ends the
correct prefix. An unfinished final number does not count. A visible correction
completed before time expires counts as corrected. Partners check afterward,
so the listener does not interrupt writing or coach during a trial.
Alphabet accuracy/rate is not a second numeric outcome. Partners note pauses
or abandoned recitation for discussion. Students prioritize both tasks and
recite continuously at a comfortable pace; no fixed alphabet rate is claimed.

ORDER
Use four sequences that balance condition positions and first-order carryover
across orders when equally represented: 1 = DS DA NA NS; 2 = DA NS DS NA;
3 = NS NA DA DS; 4 = NA DS NS DA. Actual classroom assignment may be uneven.
Number pairs 1-4 repeatedly. Partner A uses that order; B uses the next order,
wrapping 4 to 1. Each round slide lists the condition for every order.

PACING (50 MINUTES)
0-7: introduction, paper setup, scoring demonstration, predictions.
7-19: brief practice and all trials, both partners, including scoring.
19-24: entry, quick data checks, re-knit/jump to class results.
24-36: cell means, graph, main effects, simple effects, interaction.
36-45: interpretation, competing demands, design quality/variations.
45-50: exit ticket and wrap-up. Appendices are optional, outside this budget.

TIMERS
Each trial has an independent embedded 20-second timer: Start and Reset.
Timers require no internet or extra R package. They do not start automatically.
Click outside the timer before using slide-navigation keys. A timer ends with
a large STOP display; the instructor also announces stop. Reset before reuse.
If the display is unavailable, use one instructor stopwatch for the class.

NOTES
Press P in xaringan for presenter notes. Trial slides are generated by an R
helper so the eight timers and condition assignments stay consistent.
The analysis is descriptive. A nonzero sample difference in differences is
not a statistical test and is not labeled statistically significant.
-->

```{r timer, eval=FALSE, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
# An iframe isolates each timer so its script runs inside a remark slide.
# The timer uses elapsed clock time, rather than assuming every tick is exact.
timer_html <- paste0(
  '<!doctype html><html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><style>',
  'body{margin:0;font-family:Arial,sans-serif;text-align:center;background:#f3f7fb;color:#17324d}',
  '#clock{font-size:62px;font-weight:bold;line-height:1.2;margin:5px}',
  'button{font-size:20px;padding:6px 22px;margin:0 8px;border:1px solid #0072CE;',
  'border-radius:5px;background:white;color:#17324d;cursor:pointer}',
  '</style></head><body><div id="clock" role="timer" aria-live="off">', 20,
  '</div><button id="start">Start</button><button id="reset">Reset</button>',
  '<script>const duration=', 20, ';let running=false,end=0,interval;',
  'const clock=document.getElementById("clock"),start=document.getElementById("start");',
  'function tick(){const left=Math.max(0,Math.ceil((end-performance.now())/1000));',
  'clock.textContent=left===0?"STOP":left;if(left===0){clearInterval(interval);',
  'running=false;clock.style.color="#b32025";start.disabled=true;}}',
  'start.onclick=function(){if(running)return;running=true;start.disabled=true;',
  'end=performance.now()+duration*1000;tick();interval=setInterval(tick,50);};',
  'document.getElementById("reset").onclick=function(){clearInterval(interval);',
  'running=false;clock.textContent=duration;clock.style.color="";start.disabled=false;};',
  '</script></body></html>'
)
cat(as.character(htmltools::tags$iframe(
  srcdoc = timer_html, title = "20-second class timer",
  style = "width:100%;height:145px;border:0;"
)))
```

# Can You Multitask?

## A Factorial Design Challenge

---

## Roadmap

- Setup and predictions (7 min)
- Hands-on challenge with a partner (12 min)
- Score entry and class-data check (5 min)
- Class analysis: main effects and interactions (12 min)
- Interpretation and study design (9 min)
- Exit ticket and wrap-up (5 min)

--

**By the end of this lab, you should be able to:**

- Identify factors, levels, and cells in a factorial design
- Distinguish main effects from interactions
- Explain an interaction as a difference in differences
- Identify a within-groups factorial design

---

# Quick refresher: what is an interaction?

.pull-left[
- A factorial design combines levels of two or more factors.
- A **2 x 2** design has four cells.
- A main effect averages across the other factor.
]

--

.pull-right[
- An interaction asks whether the effect of one factor **depends on** the other.
- Today: does adding a second task affect writing equally with both hands?
]

---

## The Multitasking Challenge

- Objective: Experience a factorial experiment and analyze our class results

--

- Materials:
  - Paper and a pen
  - A partner
  - One class timer, run by the instructor

--

- Outcome: correct consecutive numbers written in **20 seconds**

???
The following setup, scoring, and order slides share the first 7 minutes.
Students can take an observer/recorder role if writing or speaking is
inaccessible. They still participate in predictions and analysis.

---

# Two factors, four conditions

| | Silent | Alphabet aloud |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Dominant hand** | **DS** | **DA** |
| **Non-dominant hand** | **NS** | **NA** |

- Dominant = your usual writing hand. Non-dominant = your other hand.
- In every condition, write **1, 2, 3, 4...** as far as you can.
- In alphabet conditions, say **A-Z aloud repeatedly** while writing.
- Each participant completes **all four conditions**.

---

## Multitasking Procedure

- Divide your paper into four boxes: **DS, DA, NS, NA**.

--

- Partner A writes first. Partner B listens and checks the score afterward.

--

- Start each round at **1**. Stop when the instructor says stop.

--

- Circle your score in that condition's box.

--

- After four rounds, switch roles. Each person finishes with **four scores**.

---

# What counts as the score?

Your score is the **last correctly completed number before the first sequence error**.

**Example:** 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8

--

**Score = 4.** The sequence first goes wrong when 5 is skipped.

- A repetition, out-of-order number, or unreadable number ends the correct sequence.
- An unfinished final number does not count.
- A correction completed before STOP counts as corrected.
- Check scores after the round. Keep **0** if no number was correct.

---

# Your order number

Count pairs **1, 2, 3, 4**, then repeat.

- Partner A uses the pair's number as their order.
- Partner B uses the next order, wrapping **4 back to 1**.

| Order | Round 1 | Round 2 | Round 3 | Round 4 |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 1 | DS | DA | NA | NS |
| 2 | DA | NS | DS | NA |
| 3 | NS | NA | DA | DS |
| 4 | NA | DS | NS | DA |

Write your order number on your paper. Each round slide lists your condition.

???
With equal representation, these four orders balance condition positions
and first-order carryover. Actual group sizes may be slightly uneven.
For an odd class size, a trio rotates writer/listener/recorder. Allow two
extra minutes in the activity block and shorten the discussion.

---

# Your prediction

.pull-left[
- Which condition will have the highest score?
- Will adding the alphabet affect both hands equally?
- What would that look like in a graph?
]

--

.pull-right[
**Write a prediction:**

"We predict the alphabet will have a larger effect when..."

Or explain why you expect equal effects.
]

---

# Quick practice

- Write a few numbers with each hand in the margin.
- Try writing while saying **A, B, C, D...** aloud.
- Check that both partners understand the scoring rule.

--

**During alphabet rounds:** keep both tasks going at a comfortable pace.

The listener checks that recitation continues, without interrupting or coaching.

**Practice stays in the margin. Partner A writes first.**

???
Start the 7-19 minute activity block. Keep practice under a minute.
Alphabet accuracy/rate is not a second numeric outcome. Partners note long
pauses for the later discussion. Do not require a fixed recitation rate.

| 3 | **NS**: Non-dominant + silent |
| 4 | **NA**: Non-dominant + alphabet |

# Source Code

.tiny[

```{r nom, fig.show="hide", warning=FALSE, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE}
set.seed(123) # For reproducibility

# Synthetic observations demonstrate an interaction; they are not predictions.
# Shared person effects retain the repeated-measures structure in the example.
students <- c("Tukey", "Gauss", "Noether", "Fisher", "Bayes",
              "Pearson", "Student", "Fiducial", "Neyman", "Cochran")
person <- rnorm(length(students), 0, 3)
df_syn <- tibble(
  ID = students,
  DS = pmax(0, round(42 + person + rnorm(10, 0, 2))),
  DA = pmax(0, round(35 + person + rnorm(10, 0, 2))),
  NS = pmax(0, round(28 + person + rnorm(10, 0, 2))),
  `NA` = pmax(0, round(14 + person + rnorm(10, 0, 2)))
)

# Build long-format data without treating the four rows as independent people.
df_long_syn <- df_syn %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(score_cols), names_to="Condition", values_to="Score") %>%
  mutate(Hand = if_else(str_starts(Condition, "D"), "Dominant", "Non-dominant"),
         Task = factor(if_else(str_ends(Condition, "S"), "Silent", "Alphabet"),
                       levels=c("Silent", "Alphabet")))

# Plotting the data
p_syn <- df_long_syn %>%
  group_by(Hand, Task) %>% summarise(Mean=mean(Score), .groups="drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(Task, Mean, color=Hand, group=Hand)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=1) + geom_point(size=3) +
  scale_color_manual(values=base_cols[c("Blue", "Orange")]) +
  expand_limits(y=0) +
  labs(title="Multitasking challenge (synthetic)",
       x=NULL, y="Mean correct consecutive numbers") + thm
p_syn
```

]

## Analysis in action

```{r, error=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, out.height="65%"}
library(googlesheets4)
library(tidyverse)

#Read google sheets data into R
raw <- if (nzchar(share_link)) {
  tryCatch(read_sheet(share_link), error=function(e) tibble())
} else {
  tibble()
}

# If reading fails, create an empty tibble
# Require one unique person and four valid scores for every comparison.
# Using the same complete participants in all cells preserves paired contrasts.
df <- if (!all(c("ID", score_cols) %in% names(raw))) {
  tibble(ID=character(), DS=numeric(), DA=numeric(),
         NS=numeric(), `NA`=numeric())
} else {
  raw %>%
    select(ID, all_of(score_cols)) %>%
    mutate(ID=trimws(as.character(ID)),
           across(all_of(score_cols), ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.)))) %>%
    filter(!is.na(ID), ID != "") %>%
    # Exclude every copy of a duplicated ID rather than picking one silently.
    filter(!duplicated(ID) & !duplicated(ID, fromLast=TRUE)) %>%
    filter(if_all(all_of(score_cols),
                  ~ is.finite(.) & . >= 0 & . == floor(.)))
}

# Convert the data to long format
df_long <- if (nrow(df) > 0) {
  df %>%
    pivot_longer(all_of(score_cols), names_to="Condition", values_to="Score") %>%
    mutate(Hand=factor(if_else(str_starts(Condition, "D"),
                              "Dominant", "Non-dominant"),
                       levels=c("Dominant", "Non-dominant")),
           Task=factor(if_else(str_ends(Condition, "S"), "Silent", "Alphabet"),
                       levels=c("Silent", "Alphabet")))
} else {
  tibble()
}
```

Discussion prompts:
- Did your four scores match your prediction?
- Did everyone have the same easiest and hardest conditions?

???
Private Sheets use your normal googlesheets4 authentication. A blank link,
failed read, missing headers, or no valid rows produces waiting messages.
There is no switch to synthetic data on these class-result slides.

# Our four cell means

```{r, echo=FALSE, error=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(kableExtra)

if (nrow(df_long) > 0) {
  cell_means <- df_long %>%
    group_by(Hand, Task) %>%
    summarise(Mean=mean(Score), .groups="drop")

  cell_means %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from=Task, values_from=Mean) %>%
    kable(format="html", digits=1, caption="Class data: mean writing score") %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options=c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                  full_width=FALSE) %>%
    column_spec(1, bold=TRUE)
} else {
  cat("Waiting for complete class entries...")
}
```

Higher scores mean more correct consecutive numbers in 20 seconds.

# Main Effects

.pull-left[
**Writing hand**

Average across silent and alphabet conditions for each hand.

**Adding the alphabet**

Average across dominant and non-dominant hands for each task.
]

--

.pull-right[
```{r, echo=FALSE, error=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
if (nrow(df_long) > 0) {
  marginal_means <- bind_rows(
    df_long %>% group_by(Hand) %>%
      summarise(Mean=mean(Score), .groups="drop") %>%
      transmute(Factor="Hand", Level=as.character(Hand), Mean),
    df_long %>% group_by(Task) %>%
      summarise(Mean=mean(Score), .groups="drop") %>%
      transmute(Factor="Task", Level=as.character(Task), Mean)
  )
  kable(marginal_means, format="html", digits=1) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options=c("striped", "condensed"), full_width=FALSE)
} else {
  cat("Waiting for entries...")
}
```
]

???
Ask for each marginal difference: dominant minus non-dominant, and silent
minus alphabet. These are descriptive differences, not statistical tests.

---

# Simple Effects: The Alphabet Cost

**Alphabet cost = silent score minus alphabet score.**

Calculate it separately for each hand.

```{r, echo=FALSE, error=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
if (nrow(df) > 0) {
  # Define all alphabet costs as silent minus alphabet. Positive = lower score
  # with the alphabet. Interaction is non-dominant cost minus dominant cost.
  # Individual alphabet costs, then the individual difference in differences.
  df <- df %>%
    mutate(Cost_D=DS - DA,
           Cost_N=NS - .data[["NA"]],
           Interaction=Cost_N - Cost_D)

  costs <- tibble(Hand=c("Dominant", "Non-dominant"),
                  Silent=c(mean(df$DS), mean(df$NS)),
                  Alphabet=c(mean(df$DA), mean(df[["NA"]])),
                  Cost=c(mean(df$Cost_D), mean(df$Cost_N)))
  kable(costs, format="html", digits=1) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options=c("striped", "condensed"), full_width=FALSE)
} else {
  cat("Waiting for entries...")
}
```

A positive cost means fewer correct numbers with the alphabet.

---

# Interaction: A Difference in Differences

.pull-left[
**Non-dominant alphabet cost**

minus

**Dominant alphabet cost**

$$(NS - NA) - (DS - DA)$$
]

--

.pull-right[
```{r, echo=FALSE, error=TRUE, warning=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (nrow(df) > 0) {
  # Mean of paired contrasts equals the contrast of the four cell means.
  cat(sprintf("**Class difference in differences: %.1f numbers.**",
              mean(df$Interaction)))
} else {
  cat("Waiting for entries...")
}
```

- Positive: larger alphabet cost with the non-dominant hand
- Negative: larger cost with the dominant hand
- Zero: equal costs
]

???
A nonzero sample difference does not by itself establish a statistically
supported interaction. Compare the two simple effects, rather than naming
only the highest and lowest cells. A crossover is not required.

# What Did We Learn about Our Design?

---

# What Happened When the Task Got Harder?

.pull-left[
**Writer's experience**

- Did you slow your writing?
- Did you slow the alphabet?
- Did you stop one task to keep the other going?
]

--

.pull-right[
**Listener's observations**

- Did the alphabet pause?
- Were there number-sequence errors?
- Did practice make a difference?
]

We measured writing output. We did not measure both tasks equally.

---

# Potential Limitations

.pull-left[
- **Noise:** a silent writer could still hear other people reciting.
- **Task priority:** alphabet pace might change when writing becomes harder.
]

--

.pull-right[
- **Measurement:** our score combines speed and sequence accuracy.
- **Order:** practice and fatigue can affect later rounds.
- **Reliability:** one short trial per condition leaves measurement noise.
]

Which limitation would you address first, and how?

---

# Relating to Factorial Designs

.pull-left[
**Today's within-groups design**

Each person completes all four hand/task combinations.

**Between-groups alternative**

Each person completes one randomly assigned combination.
]

--

.pull-right[
**Mixed alternative**

Assign each person one hand, then have them complete both task conditions.

Which design needs more people to have the same number of observations in each cell?
]

---

# Exit Ticket

1. Identify the factorial notation and which factors are within-groups.
2. Calculate the class difference in differences from the four cell means.
3. Explain the result in one sentence about how the alphabet effect depends on hand.
4. Identify one limitation and a change that would address it.

???
Start the 45-50 minute exit/wrap-up block. Answer 1: 2 x 2, both within-groups.
For the contrast, use (NS - NA) - (DS - DA). Accept a reversed sign when
consistently defined and interpreted. Similar costs are a valid result.

---

# Wrapping Up...

.pull-left[
## Key Takeaways

1. Two factors with two levels create four cells.
2. A main effect averages across the other factor.
3. An interaction compares the effects at different levels of the other factor.
]

.pull-right[
## Our Central Question

Does adding a second task affect writing equally with both hands?

**The answer comes from a difference in differences.**
]
